title: Flowers of Ferdinand

beds.name: Path Bed
beds.aspect: North-west corner, out by the street
beds.description: North-west corner, out by the street and clear of the house. Being simplified: the sage and rosemary are coming out, the tulips are lifted, and the bearded iris is going too, which leaves shasta daisies and black-eyed Susans with the bed to themselves. Full sun and sharp drainage, which is what the herbs were thriving on, so the ground where they stood wants compost worked through it before the black-eyed Susans go in.

plan.goal: Two plants, one long summer, and almost nothing to do between times.

method.title: Lift the bearded iris while the window is open
method.when: Now, it closes in early September
method.body: Removal itself can happen any time, but this is the last week the rhizomes come up as firm divisions rather than a clump for the bin. Cut the leaves to a six inch fan, snap the rhizomes apart, keep what is firm and pass it on. Clear every old leaf off the ground while you are there, because iris leaf spot overwinters on dead foliage and this bed is about to be replanted.

method.title: Dig the herb stumps out after the first proper rain
method.body: Not in August. A woody root ball comes out of damp ground with a fraction of the effort, and nothing suffers by waiting. Get the roots out rather than leaving them to rot in place, since that is exactly where the new planting goes.

method.title: Work compost into where the herbs stood
method.body: That corner grew Mediterranean herbs for years, which want it lean and dry, and black-eyed Susans want more moisture than that. A couple of buckets forked through the top spit. With the iris gone there is nothing left here that rots under compost, so the improving and the planting no longer pull against each other.

method.title: Plant the black-eyed Susans
method.when: Autumn if you can get plants, spring otherwise
method.body: Autumn is the better window here: warm soil, the rains arrive to do the establishing, and you barely water. Buy the clumping perennial kinds such as 'Goldsturm'. Do not feed beyond the compost. Fed rudbeckia flops, and so does shasta daisy, and this bed is exposed.

method.title: Divide both, on the same clock
method.when: Early spring, about every three years
method.body: This is the whole maintenance of the bed and the reason the pairing is worth having. Both want dividing on roughly the same cycle, both want it in early spring rather than autumn, and both want an inch of compost and nothing else. One date, one job, the entire bed.

watch: Nothing flowers here between October and June. That is the real cost of simplifying, and it lands in the bed most visible from the street. Daffodils planted under the perennials would cover March and April, ask nothing after planting, and already return and multiply in the front beds. Not planted, and not decided.
Flopping, with a dead centre and the flowers pushed out to the edges, is the shasta daisy asking to be divided. That is the three year clock telling you it is due.

Angular brown or black spots climbing up the lower leaves of the black-eyed Susan is Septoria leaf spot, which rudbeckia get badly in this climate. Take the affected leaves off, water the soil rather than the foliage, and clear every dead leaf in autumn.

beds.name: Street Bed Box 1
beds.description: The cut-flower box. Dahlias, gaillardia, scabiosa, cosmos and sunflowers, all still going. Needs constant deadheading for the next ten weeks.

beds.name: Street Bed Box 2
beds.description: Mostly finished and holding a lot of seed. One good clearing pass now, then it becomes the place hardy annuals get sown in September.

beds.name: Driveway Bed 1
beds.description: North-east corner beyond the driveway, out by the street and clear of the house. The annual patch: sunflowers, zinnias and a wildflower mix, grown here on purpose and staying that way. All three want full sun, which is the evidence for the sun rating.

plan.goal: Stout single stems and big heads, not a thicket of thin ones.

method.title: Keep sowing in fall
method.body: This already works here and it is the reason the patch comes up strong, so it stays. The seed sits through winter and germinates the week the soil is ready, which is earlier than you would dare sow by hand, and the taproot is never disturbed. Anything started in a pot in May is behind before it goes in.

method.title: Get the seedlings past the slugs
method.when: The first three weeks after they emerge
method.body: This is where a fall-sown patch is won or lost. The seedlings come up into a wet spring, which is peak slug season, and a sunflower at two leaves is one night's work. Check every couple of days from first emergence until they are hand height. After that they are too tough to matter.

method.title: Thin, and harder than feels reasonable
method.when: At four to six inches tall
method.body: This is the whole answer to scraggly. Volunteers come up in clumps where the heads fell, and ten seedlings in a hand's width gives you ten thin whippy stems with small heads, every time. Thin to eighteen inches apart for the single-stem types and twelve for the branching one. Cut the extras off at soil level instead of pulling, so you do not tear the roots of the one you are keeping.

method.title: Water deep, and not often
method.body: Deep and infrequent drives the taproot down, and a deep taproot is what makes a tall sunflower stand up by itself in an exposed spot out by the street. A daily splash keeps the roots near the surface and gives you exactly the leaning you are trying to avoid. One long slow soak a week beats a short one every day.

method.title: Earth up the tall ones
method.body: Draw soil up around the base of the big single-stem plants. It anchors them, and it is far quicker than staking a whole patch.

watch: Thin stems with small heads. In a bed this sunny that is crowding, not light, and it means the thinning did not happen or did not go far enough.
Powdery mildew, which crowding causes too by killing air movement. Thinning fixes the mildew and the scraggly stems in one job.

The branching yellow will never be one tall stout stalk. That is what a branching variety is: many smaller flowers on thinner stems, by design. If tall and strong is the goal, save seed from the mahogany, and buy a single-stem mammoth type to sow alongside it.

beds.name: Front Lower Bed
beds.aspect: North side, street level below the retaining wall
beds.description: The wooden-edged strip at street level, packed with tulips in March and April. I had this down as shade and said sun-lovers would disappoint here, which the photographs flatly contradict. Two things I did not know: the front is terraced, so these beds sit raised and clear of the worst of the house shadow, and a north aspect still gets real early and late sun through spring and summer, when the sun rises and sets well north of east and west. It is shaded around midday and in winter, which is exactly why a spring display works so well here.

beds.name: Upper Bed
beds.aspect: North side, raised above the retaining wall
beds.description: The raised bed above the retaining wall, and by a distance the fullest planting in the garden. Nineteen things recorded so far and probably not all of them. Tulips, primroses, violas, English daisies, dianthus and sweet william over a base of candytuft and creeping mats, with hostas and bleeding heart in the shadier ground under the maple, clematis on the trellis behind, and periwinkle spilling down the wall face. Baby's breath and flax carry it past the bulbs into early summer. Raised and free-draining, which is why the cushion-forming plants do so well here.

beds.name: Side Bed Box
beds.description: Narrow raised bed on the west wall. Strawberries, beans on string trellis, sunflowers and the compost tumbler. West facing means shade until around midday, then several hours of strong afternoon sun with heat radiating off the wall and held in it overnight. Add a foundation that wicks moisture away and an eave that keeps rain off, and you get warm still air over dry roots, which is what powdery mildew wants. Hotter and drier than it looks.

beds.name: Driveway Bed 2
beds.description: East of the driveway alongside the house. Sunflowers, zinnias and gladiolus, and confirmed as full sun, which is more than its position beside the house suggested: nothing tall stands to the east of it. Together with Driveway Bed 1 it makes the driveway side a second sunny run rather than the marginal strip the map implied.

plan.goal: The same sunflower patch as Driveway Bed 1, worked around the gladiolus.

method.title: Run the Driveway Bed 1 method
method.body: Fall sowing, slug watch on the seedlings, hard thinning at four to six inches, deep infrequent water. Nothing about it changes for being the narrower bed.

method.title: Keep the sunflowers off the gladiolus
method.body: This bed is narrow, and a thinned sunflower at eighteen inches across will shade a gladiolus fan completely. Thin so the sunflowers sit on the outer edge and the corms keep their light, rather than thinning evenly across the whole width.

method.title: Lift the corms without disturbing the taproots
method.body: The gladiolus lift and the fall sunflower sowing land in the same weeks. Lift the corms first, then sow, so you are not digging through seed you just put down.

watch: Gladiolus going all leaf and no spike, which in this bed usually means the sunflowers next to them got too close.
The same crowding signs as Driveway Bed 1: thin stems, small heads, mildew.

beds.name: Back Bed 2
beds.aspect: East side of the house, south end
beds.description: Narrow bed wrapping the south-east corner of the house, between the house and the stairs. The plan draws it as an L: the leg shown here plus an arm running west along the back of the house. Morning light at best and hemmed in on several sides. Not seen yet.

beds.name: Back Bed 1
beds.aspect: South-east corner, on the neighbour boundary
beds.description: The far south-east corner, against the neighbouring property. South facing, which is promising, but narrow and boxed in. Not seen yet.

beds.name: Back Bed 3
beds.description: A south wall would normally make this the best growing spot on the property, but two or three storey townhomes stand close to the south across the easement and they block the low sun. At Seattle's latitude the sun only clears a building that tall and that close for a few hours around midday between roughly May and July, and from September through March this bed gets essentially nothing. It is warm sheltered shade rather than a hot bed: the wall holds heat, but boxed in on both sides means still air, so expect mildew pressure like the side bed.

footnote: Ticking a box here is a local convenience for working at the bed. The durable record is content/plan.json. Frost timing is a ten-year average for in-city Seattle and varies by several weeks year to year, so treat November as a watch-the-forecast month rather than a dated one.
